title: Ten Keys to Great PD
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart Jr. synthesizes nearly two decades of experience as both a recipient and facilitator of professional development into ten principles that distinguish career-changing PD from the forgettable kind. He argues that effective PD shares features with effective teaching: it focuses on one simple, fundamental idea; treats underlying rationale, not just method; is deliberately repetitive because repetition signals importance and creates space for multiple drafts of learning; and emerges from the presenter's firsthand experience. He further specifies that great PD involves writing or discussion, remains manageable within a teacher's existing workload, must pass a 'More Learning, Less Stress' test, and closes with actionable human-shaping takeaways rather than checklists. The article implicitly argues that PD designers who ignore these principles are asking teachers to receive new knowledge in contexts that violate every principle of good learning.
points: Effective PD focuses on one fundamental, timeless idea per session — something that will benefit teachers not just this year but for many years — rather than attempting comprehensive framework installation.

Deliberate repetition is a feature, not a flaw: it signals that the idea is important, creates space for multiple drafts of understanding, and models the principle that deeply simple ideas repay sustained attention.

Writing is the most efficient mechanism for transforming understanding in PD, just as in student learning; PD that includes writing (or substantive discussion as a lesser alternative) produces deeper change than passive listening.

Every proposed PD action step should pass a 'More Learning, Less Stress' test — if it doesn't seem likely to do both simultaneously, teachers shouldn't adopt it and PD designers shouldn't recommend it.

The most effective PD gives teachers a tool they understand and teaches them to treat using it as an ongoing learning experience — producing human-shaping change rather than a mindless checklist item.
quotes: As I approach the 20-year mark of my career in education, I've probably spent thousands of hours thinking about, experiencing, or leading professional development experiences. Lots of them have been…not so great. But some of them? Career-changing.

The most impactful PD book I've read has probably been Mike Schmoker's book Focus. The man is relentlessly repetitive on his three things schools can do to get better. The repetition works. It signals importance. It signals there's more to learn in the seemingly simple and fundamental things that are being repeated.

Writing is the most efficient means for transforming the human mind. This is why my students write so much, mostly in the provisional mode of writing. It's also why I write so much. It's impossible to multi-task while writing, so it forces concentration. Writing is exploratory. It is generative.

Listen, colleague: my work is all about these four words. If something I share with you today doesn't seem likely to both produce more learning and reduce stress, don't do it. You don't need one more thing to do unless it can meet both those criteria. I don't either.

Give me a thing to mindlessly check off a list, and you won't change me. Give me a tool to use that I understand and teach me to treat this tool like a learning experience, and now you might end up changing me.
The most efficient means to change the world is by changing human beings; human beings change very reliably when you shape the mind and put ideas into practice.
